To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the detection threshold of a curve in a noisy image is a function of the length of that curve and the complexity of its search space.

(1) The detection threshold of a straight edge of length L is proportional to the square root of the product of L and the number of candidate edge orientations, (2) the detection threshold of a curved edge of length L and curvature radius R is proportional to the product of L, the number of candidate orientations, and the square root of R, and (3) the detection of faint edges is facilitated by the use of difference filters that are constructed to match the curves traced out by these edges

(i) the detection threshold of an edge is a monotonically increasing function of the length of the sought edge; (ii) this function is independent of image intensity and noise statistics; (iii) the detection threshold can be significantly lowered by increasing the search space; and (iv) these findings can be used to develop computationally efficient edge detectors for faint edges in noisy and blurred images.
